background.definition: Episcleritis is characterized by edema and injection confined to the episcleral tissue and is typically benign. In scleritis, there is edema in the episcleral and scleral tissues with injection in both superficial and deep episcleral vessels. Scleritis can be chronic, recurrent, and vision threatening.

list.listitem: Uncertain incidence but uncommon.

A systematic review of 74 studies found an incidence of 2.7 per 100,000 in ophthalmologic centers and 1.4 per 100,000 in population-based studies. It was more common in women than in men (67% vs 33%) and the average age at diagnosis was 48 years.

A variety of collagen vascular diseases: rheumatoid arthritis, systemic vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa, giant cell arteritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Reiter's syndrome, psoriatic arthritis, and other rheumatic disease.

list.listitem: Episcleritis typically presents with a red eye without accompanying pain, discharge, or vision loss. There is occasionally foreign body sensation, but any pain beyond this should lead to the suspicion of scleritis.

The typical case of scleritis has a subacute onset of pain and tenderness in the eye. The eye will be described as red, but the inflammation usually has a violet appearance. Visual changes and light sensitivity can accompany scleritis and often indicate spillover intraocular inflammation.Patients describe a severe ache or boring type of pain and tenderness that can awaken them from sleep.

A complete ophthalmic examination is required to evaluate intraocular pressure, intraocular inflammation, and retinal changes. Application of phenylephrine 10% should lead to blanching of episcleritis but not scleritis.
Review of systems and a general medical physical examination are needed to help guide a systemic laboratory work-up.

A diagnosis of scleritis mandates laboratory evaluation for systemic disease, because 44% of patients with scleritis have an underlying disease (7% are infectious, 37% rheumatic). Approximately 3 of 4 with an underlying disease already have a diagnosis when scleritis presents. Systemic vasculitis is most likely to be undiagnosed at the time of scleritis presentation.
Order complete blood count to evaluate for infection.

Order ESR or CRP if giant cell arteritis is suspected, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) and rheumatoid factor if lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disorder, rheumatoid arthritis, or polymyositis is suspected.
Order c-ANCA and p-ANCA if Wegener's or polyarteritis nodosa clinically is suspected.

Other potentially useful tests depending on clinical presentation include HLA-B27 (spondyloarthropathies), anti-DNA antibodies (systemic lupus erythematosus), IgE (Churg-Strauss or atopy), urinalysis to look for casts, serum uric acid (gout), syphilis serology, chest x-ray (TB and vasculitis), and sarcoidosis screen with serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and or lysozyme.
Additional laboratory testing as indicated from review of systems and general physical based on differential diagnosis.
Suspect scleritis or episcleritis in a patient with red or violet eye, especially if history of autoimmune or collagen vascular disease.
Differentiation of episcleritis and scleritis is made on clinical grounds based on patient symptoms and examination findings.
See algorithm in .
For scleritis of the nonnecrotizing variety, consider a trial of prednisolone acetate 1% every 1 to 2 hours C versus oral NSAIDs such as indomethacin or celecoxib. B
If there is failure or necrotizing, use oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/d. B
If there is failure, use local steroid injection versus systemic immunosuppressive drug such as cyclophosphamide or tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors. B

Treatment of episcleritis is stepwise. Episcleritis is usually self-limited and rarely results in visual loss (2%), so care must be taken not to overtreat. Treatment begins with observation alone or artificial tears; 80% of patients will have complete resolution of symptoms by 3 weeks without treatment. If there is no response, then a 1-week course of fluorometholone 0.1% drops 4 times per day followed by a taper over another 2 weeks is appropriate. If this fails then a stronger topical steroid such as prednisolone acetate 1% 4 times per day may be used. Intraocular pressure monitoring is a must with steroid use. If this fails, an oral NSAID (classically indomethacin) can be used. When using systemic NSAIDs, GI prophylaxis with a histamine blocker or proton pump inhibitor is a must. Randomized trials have shown only a slightly higher cure rate with topical agents compared with placebo.

Scleritis of the nonnecrotizing variety can initially be treated with either topical prednisolone acetate 1% every 1 to 2 hours (success rate of 47% over 2 months) in mild cases or oral NSAIDs (classically indomethacin 25 mg 4 times per day, although celecoxib has been used with a response rate of 91%). If this fails to bring the inflammation under control in 2 weeks, an alternative NSAID may be used. If the patient fails to respond, oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/d should be used. A controversial alternative to oral prednisone is the use of a local steroid injection. Steroid failure necessitates the use of a systemic immunosuppressive drug such as cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, cyclosporine, azathioprine, or TNF inhibitors.
Biologic agents such as tofacitinib and upadacitinib are increasingly used based on case series primarily.
Low quality evidence supports use of 0.1% topical tacrolimus for nodular scleritis.

In necrotizing scleritis, NSAIDs are not effective, and oral steroids and/or systemic immunosuppressives should be used first line. Patients with systemic vasculitis need appropriate systemic therapy for the vasculitis (cyclophosphamide).
See for treatment of episcleritis and scleritis.
Local steroid injection can be used if initial therapy fails.
Scleral patching is occasionally needed for severe necrotizing scleritis for reinforcement of ocular tissue.
Conjunctival resection can be useful for associated corneal melting.
Use culture or biopsy if infectious etiology is suspected.
When using systemic agents, always remember GI prophylaxis, prophylaxis against osteoporosis for long-term steroid users, and systemic monitoring of side effects.
Patients with scleritis should always be referred to an ophthalmologist for evaluation.
Systemic work-up should be carried out for scleritis.
Immunomodulation medications should be carefully monitored.
Decreased vision occurs in 2% of patients with episcleritis. B
Decreased vision occurs in 37% of patients with scleritis. B

cell.label: Red eye. Examine eye and ocular adnexa.
Redness; no pain or foreign body sensation only; blanches with phenylephrine 10%?
Trial of no treatment or artificial tears 4 times per day and prn.
Fluorometholone 0.1% 1 drop 4 times per day for 1 wk, followed by taper over 2 wk. (Okay to substitute other steroid such as loteprednol or prednisolone acetate.)
Violet hue more than redness; scleral edema; tenderness; vision change; failure to blanch with phenylephrine 10%?
Complete ophthalmic examination and systemic evaluation. Treat underlying disease if any.
Topical prednisolone acetate 1% every 1-2 h or oral NSAID (indomethacin or ibuprofen or other).
Systemic steroid (prednisone 1 mg/kg/d) versus peribulbar steroid injection.
Systemic immunosuppression (methotrexate, cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, TNF inhibitors).
